claims.text: A machine-learning model trained on diverse experimental and simulation data can optimize processing parameters in multi-component alloys.
Model-guided processing can refine microstructure, improve phase stability, and optimize alloy properties.
Refractory high-entropy alloys are examples of multi-component alloys to which the proposed approach could be applied.
Conventionally processed multi-component alloys have coarser microstructures.
Conventionally processed multi-component alloys contain equilibrium phases.
Machine learning can correlate processing conditions with resulting microstructural features and properties.
Mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, and high-pressure/high-temperature treatments are suitable processing routes for the proposed model-guided optimization.
The applicable processing domain includes ranges of milling time, sintering parameters, and pressure-temperature regimes typical of advanced alloy synthesis.
Grain size, phase composition, and short-range ordering are microstructural attributes relevant to phase stability and mechanical behavior.
A machine-learning model can integrate multimodal datasets to identify processing-structure-property relationships.
Predicted adjustment of processing parameters can induce grain refinement and stabilize desired phases.
Grain refinement and stabilization of desired phases will optimize mechanical performance.
Alloys processed under model-guided conditions will have finer microstructures than alloys produced through traditional trial-and-error processing.
Alloys processed under model-guided conditions will have greater phase stability than conventionally processed samples.
Alloys processed under model-guided conditions will exhibit higher strength and ductility than conventionally processed samples.
Model efficacy is limited to the compositions and processing parameters represented in its training data.
Predictions may be less accurate when extrapolated to new alloy systems, new compositional spaces, or extreme processing conditions.
Further experimental validation is required before universal applicability can be established.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing model-guided and conventional-processing batches using grain-size, phase-composition, hardness, and tensile measurements.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in phase stability, grain refinement, and mechanical properties relative to the conventional batch would falsify the hypothesis.
